core_conclusion: Cities historically improved through a four-step learning loop in which disruption produced evidence, evidence generated pressure, and pressure forced governing agencies to modify rules - the Great Fire of London (1666) yielded building regulations within two years, and repeated Rhine and Danube flooding produced the zoning and hazard-mapping standards now common in European planning. The author argues this loop is degrading on every inhabited continent, replaced by a 'volatile urbanism' in which cities change constantly but no longer accumulate adaptation, so resilience erodes.
why_it_matters: Relocates resilience failure from infrastructure to institutional learning capacity; specifies a four-link mechanism whose steps can be instrumented and tested independently; introduces 'volatile urbanism' to distinguish rapid change from cumulative adaptation; frames a quantifiable tipping condition in which hazard frequency outpaces regulatory learning latency.
why_nature: Agenda-setting single-page commentary format suited to Science's front matter; cross-disciplinary reach spanning urban planning, disaster science, political science and climate adaptation; timely against compounding climate hazards; policy-facing with concrete institutional targets; supplies a portable conceptual coinage ('volatile urbanism') that seeds follow-up empirical work.
